title: Jack Kilby and the Circuit That Fit on a Sliver of Germanium
summary: When Jack Kilby switched on an oscillator at Texas Instruments in September 1958, a sliver of germanium produced a steady electrical signal. Its fine gold wires tell another part of the story. They made the demonstration work, but each connection still had to be made by hand. Kilby’s route from a Kansas ice storm to that Dallas laboratory helps explain why he thought an entire circuit could be built from semiconductor material. Robert Noyce, Jean Hoerni and a team at Fairchild found a way to put the wiring into the manufacturing process itself. This biography follows those distinct achievements into a calculator that printed its answers on paper and, decades later, into the processors that run neural networks. Across those devices a practical question keeps returning. How far must an electrical signal travel to do useful work?

title: What can you safely tell AI at work?
summary: When Bhaskar Bharat Sawant troubleshoots a software problem, an error message often provides the first clue. It can also present a dilemma: how much of that message can he safely share with AI tools? Sawant, a lead engineer and solution architect at building-products manufacturer Cornerstone Building Brands, works with legacy applications and newer technologies. GenAI can help explain an error or suggest a way forward. But the input it needs to understand the problem may expose personally identifiable information, a customer’s competitive secrets, or his own company’s proprietary information. “Logs or error messages can reveal internal service names, configuration details, or business processes,” Sawant said. “You have to protect that information whether it belongs to your employer or a customer.” A customer’s name is an obvious identifier. A method name, file path, or sequence of requests between systems is less conspicuous. Together, those details can expose how an application works or how a business operates — even when no individual can be identified. Sawant’s approach is to construct a smaller, fictional version of the problem. “I create a small code example with made-up data that reproduces the issue,” he said. “Then I ask myself whether someone outside the company could piece together proprietary information from it. If they could, I simplify it further or keep it out of the AI tool.” That process takes judgment and effort before AI can save him any time. It also exposes the difficulty behind a simple workplace instruction: don’t share confidential or sensitive information with generative AI. Employees must translate that warning into decisions about actual work, often while trying to meet a deadline. What remains after you remove the names Employees can recognize the need to protect information and still overlook what they are sharing. title: Everything you always wanted to know about Secure Exclaves but were afraid to ask
summary: We were first publicly introduced to Secure Exclaves when Apple introduced Siri Recap with watchOS 26 . Now a recently published Apple security research paper sees them discussed as a protection for person recognition in HomeView . They are part of a new security architecture designed to protect user privacy even while computing becomes more ambient, smarter, and more pervasive. While it’s good that Apple is thinking about such things, there is no guarantee at all that other companies, or even governments, will take steps to protect people’s privacy as what are effectively surveillance technologies go mainstream. So, what are Secure Exclaves? Secure Exclaves are compartmentalized runtimes that make up a new security architecture in Apple silicon. The system uses an Apple-customized L4 microkernel, originally built for deployments like the Secure Enclave Processor. This provides a highly isolated environment in which to process camera and microphone data in such a way that only specific metadata is shared with the main operating system. The idea behind this is that this information is not stored, shared, or digitized in the conventional sense, even while the data itself can be processed. All that is stored is the condensed text and summary. One way to think about this is that even if you end up with a summarized note concerning the meeting, the raw data of the meeting itself is never stored, which means — Apple claims — it can’t be accessed by your devices, Apple, or anyone else. (Though the summary text that is created can be accessed.) Overall, it’s an architecture that lets AI work with data on the fly, working only with the real-life data stream most of the time. There are two primary modes for the tech: ambient and active. When in ambient mode, only specific information can be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, such as a Siri conversation or a FaceTime call, data can be released to the main OS, with a secure indicator (usually a physical light)

title: Who found the 303 new figures in the Nazca desert?
summary: From the air, a faint outline on the Nazca pampa can look like a figure or an accident of the desert surface. Deciding which outlines deserve a visit is half the work. In six months of fieldwork, archaeologists documented 303 previously unrecorded figurative geoglyphs. A model had marked 178 of them individually in aerial photographs. Another 66 came to light beside a figure it had flagged. The remaining 59 emerged through other field observations or through inspection of photographs outside the marked areas. Put those figures back on the map and a different question comes into view. Many of the smaller reliefs lie close to winding trails. Someone crossing the pampa on foot could have seen images of people and domesticated animals along the way. Where a figure stood helps us imagine who might have seen it. What it meant to that traveller is a harder question, one the field team leaves open.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When a Greek inscription breaks, who supplies the missing letters?
summary: A piece of a Greek decree breaks away just where an official’s name should be. Two names fit the space. Which one belongs in the next edition? To find out whether a computer could help a historian make that choice, researchers hid letters in inscriptions whose wording was already known. Two specialists could search other Greek texts for similar phrases. When they also had twenty suggested readings from Ithaca, their accuracy in restoring the whole missing sequence rose from about one quarter to nearly three quarters. An editor facing a real stone has no answer sheet. A name that appears on dozens of decrees may belong to someone who held office a century too late. A rarer name may fit both the surviving letters and the history of the city. The brackets around a restored name preserve that distinction for everyone who reads the inscription next.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Claude Shannon
summary: As a boy in Michigan, Claude Shannon built a telegraph with a friend so that they could send messages between their homes. At Bell Laboratories he later asked how reliably any message could travel over a noisy line. His answer gave engineers a way to measure information and established a limit to what a channel can carry. Shannon also wanted to know how a machine could learn from its own experience. In a filmed demonstration, a mechanical mouse found its way through a maze and remembered the route. The memory lay beneath the floor, in telephone relays wired in large part by mathematician Betty Moore Shannon. From the switches of his early circuits to a chess player weighing its next move, the biography follows questions Shannon could put to a practical test. In his toy room, a juggling machine had to catch the balls it threw.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Carver Mead and the Eye Made of Silicon
summary: When Carver Mead received a lifetime award for neuromorphic engineering, he used his speech to credit the student who had persuaded him to build a silicon retina. Misha Mahowald’s question suited an engineer who had grown up beside a hydroelectric plant and later helped students design chips of their own. Could the connections between electronic components do some of the work of seeing? Their experimental retina compared light across neighbouring points. A second collaboration, with Richard Lyon, produced a circuit that separated sounds according to frequency. This biography follows Mead from the design rules he developed with Lynn Conway to experiments that a reader can picture with a pencil line and a sheet of paper. It also follows those questions into a listening device and a table-tennis robot, where electrical power and the time taken to find a moving ball can both be measured.
author: The Bible of AI

title: What does an AI chip do between events? Inside neuromorphic vision
summary: An event camera watching a doorway can report a change at the edge of a moving coat while the stationary doorframe generates little traffic. What does a neuromorphic chip do with that difference, and how much electricity can it save over a quiet hour? Two experiments offer a way to answer. Speck puts a vision sensor and a spiking processor on one chip. Its gesture recognition measurements show how filtering events changes both power and accuracy. A separate object detection study compares Intel’s Loihi 2 with a Jetson Orin Nano and finds different winners for energy per inference and detection rate. Following a single crossing from a pixel to an alarm reveals what those comparisons leave open. A practical test would count timely detections and false alarms while measuring energy at the supply for the complete device.
author: The Bible of AI

title: What happens when Canon’s wafer stage brakes? Recovering energy to make memory for AI
summary: A lithography scanner spends electricity moving a silicon wafer from one exposure field to the next. What happens to that energy when the stage slows down? Canon’s FPA-6400ES6a captures part of it for reuse. Canon reports lower electricity consumption per wafer than its preceding KrF scanner and specifies 400 wafer passes per hour under a defined exposure recipe. We follow the energy through one braking cycle and examine why a faster machine can use less electricity per wafer yet draw more power over a busy shift. The distinction matters for factories making memory for AI accelerators. A useful comparison would measure electrical energy at the machine inlet, alignment on the patterned wafers and the number of memory dies that pass electrical tests. Those measurements would show how much of the benefit reaches the supply of usable memory.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Where does power enter a nanosheet transistor? The case of TSMC A16
summary: Where does the supply current enter a transistor built from stacked sheets of silicon? TSMC’s A16 process brings power to the device from the back of the wafer. That change can leave more room above it for the wires that carry signals between logic cells. It also explains how a manufacturer can report higher chip density while preserving gate density. This review follows the contact from the supply rail to the transistor and checks the comparison with TSMC’s N2P process. Two reports give the same range for a speed gain while holding different electrical quantities constant. A separate simulation from imec shows why the choice of contact can matter more as cells become shorter. For an AI accelerator, the decisive questions are how much of a workload waits for logic, how much waits for memory, and how much energy the whole system spends on each completed inference.
author: The Bible of AI

title: How AI is warping both developers and developer tools
summary: By now you’ve no doubt heard of the ArtCraft software collection , where a group of developers used AI-powered software development tools to build feature-exact clones of the Adobe Creative Suite — and the Microsoft Office suite, and the AutoDesk CAD applications, and the list goes on. But for me the most striking app ArtCraft has released so far isn’t a clone of an existing app. It’s a relatively original project called Craft Anything — essentially a fancy agent harness for studying existing applications or websites, then prompting an LLM to create your own copy of it, either by reproducing its outward behavior (“clean-room” cloning, as they call it) or by disassembling binaries. You never have to touch a line of code if you don’t want to. It’s the “no-code” dream, pushed to the limit. We’ve sensed for some time now that with LLM-driven development, anyone can theoretically whip up their own clone of a software program with no programming. What we’re not yet appreciating, I think, is two other consequences: That attitude is driving the development of ever-more-abstracted software tools, and transforming existing software tools into more abstracted ones. That attitude is also fostering new generations of developers for whom those tools will be their first contact with programming. And possibly also their last. Let’s start with the tools. Once upon a time, when dinosaurs roamed the earth and programs lived on paper tape and punch cards, the distance between the programs one wrote and the machines they ran on was very small. Eventually, higher-level languages allowed developers to tackle their problems using human-readable syntax instead of wrangling with hardware-specific machine code. Stories abounded about how the first compilers were received with mixed feelings, because of the abstractions they imposed over the machine. title: How AI agents are changing the rules of software governance
summary: The conversation around AI governance is already happening. Organizations have spent the past few years accelerating AI adoption across software development. Now they face a different problem. AI systems can act faster than the organizations responsible for them can understand or govern what is happening. Organizations are thinking about compliance, data privacy, security, and model reliability while boards are demanding policies and regulators are developing frameworks. The challenge now is how to turn those newly implemented levers into tangible controls that work at the pace of today’s AI-driven software development without creating a bottleneck. AI has significantly lowered the barriers to generating code. Assistants can suggest individual functions, while increasingly capable coding agents can work across repositories, run tests, make changes, and execute multi-step development tasks. For software development organizations, the goal now is to scale AI across development workflows while ensuring that the people ultimately responsible for the software can still understand, verify, and stand behind what those systems produce. AI is changing the developer workflow Traditionally, AI assistants operate within relatively clear boundaries such as a coding assistant recommending certain functions or completing a section of code. Agents, however, operate entirely differently. Rather than responding to a single prompt, they can perform multi-step workflows. They can access tools, retrieve data, write code, trigger actions and coordinate tasks on behalf of users. For engineering teams, the ability for AI to increasingly take action within developer environments is the most profound change in how they work. When a developer accepts an AI-generated code suggestion, accountability is seemingly straightforward. title: Getting started with AG-UI — the agent-user interaction protocol
summary: While AI agents, which can perform long-running work autonomously, have supplanted simple chats for serious work with large (and small) language models, agents have a last-mile problem: How do you display what an agent is doing in front of a user and let the user act on it, without forcing every team to build its own plumbing? One answer is AG-UI , which is intended to standardize how AI agents connect to user-facing applications. AG-UI was developed based on real-world requirements and practical experience. It grew out of CopilotKit’s initial partnership with LangChain and CrewAI, but has grown to support most of the major agent frameworks. What are AI agents, exactly? An AI agent is like a self-driving car for computers—it’s a software system that uses artificial intelligence to think, make plans, and do several things in a row to get what it wants. Unlike a typical chatbot that responds to a single question, an AI agent can engage in a continuous cycle of thinking, utilizing tools, analyzing outcomes, and refining its approach for the next iteration. AI agents have a brain (usually a large language model, LLM); hands (tools that can access web browsers, APIs, or code execution); memory (short-term context in RAM, and long-term context in a database, typically a vector database); and an orchestrator (a manager for the workflow, loops, and communication between steps). What are agent frameworks? Agent frameworks are software toolkits that help you to build agents. Some of the most important agent frameworks are shown in the table below. An AI agent framework is a collection of software tools, libraries, and architectural building blocks that assist developers in designing, orchestrating, and executing autonomous AI systems. An agent framework offers the infrastructure for an LLM to reason, plan, utilize tools, retain past interactions, and execute multi-step workflows, rather than simply prompting it to generate text in a single turn. summary: Following a roughly day-long global outage of many Microsoft services last week, Microsoft on Monday issued a preliminary post-incident report that identified multiple causes for the issues, including the admission that the environment used to test the underlying problematic software update did not match the actual infrastructure it would run on. The report, a summary of which was posted on social media by Microsoft EVP Charles Lamanna, identified some of the factors that cascaded to cause the outage. “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions,” the report said, adding, “this defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.” Its deployment began in July, and, the report said, “for more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact.” Microsoft admitted that, although it did test the change before deployment, its test environment didn’t match reality. “Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs,” it said. “The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.” A surge in traffic caused by unrelated issues also helped trigger the problem and delay it from being fixed, the company explained. “Within Microsoft 365, we maintain two independent and heterogenous network gateway systems designed for isolation and high availability,” Microsoft said. “This allows many Microsoft 365 services to fail to/from them during outages or disruptions. Approximately fifteen hours before the outage, Teams failed over from the alternative networking gateway to the primary gateway that also supports Exchange Online. title: llm 0.37.3
summary: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp
